stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle on the south side of Elm Street and the east side of Diagonal Avenue?
stimulus: In a city's street plan, Elm Street and Oak Street are straight and parallel, and Elm Street lies north of Oak Street. Diagonal Avenue is a straight road that crosses both streets. Where the avenue crosses Elm Street, the angle on the north side of Elm Street and the east side of the avenue measures $(4x + 12)^\circ$. Where the avenue crosses Oak Street, the angle on the south side of Oak Street and the west side of the avenue measures $(6x - 28)^\circ$.
explanation: Sketch the two parallel streets and the avenue, and label the four angles at each crossing by compass position. At the Oak Street crossing, the south-west angle is vertical to the north-east angle, so the two are equal. Because the streets are parallel, the north-east angle at Oak equals the north-east angle at Elm (corresponding angles). So the two marked angles are equal: $4x + 12 = 6x - 28$, which gives $x = 20$. Each marked angle is therefore $4(20) + 12 = 92^\circ$. The angle you are asked for, south side of Elm and east side of the avenue, forms a linear pair with the $92^\circ$ angle along Elm Street. Its measure is $180 - 92 = 88^\circ$.

common_errors.why: Found the measure of the marked angle at Elm Street and stopped there, instead of finding the angle next to it on the other side of Elm Street.
Solved for x correctly and gave that value instead of an angle measure.
Treated the two marked angles as supplementary. That gives $10x - 16 = 180$, so $x = 19.6$, a marked angle of $90.4^\circ$, and $180 - 90.4 = 89.6$.
Treated the marked angles as supplementary ($x = 19.6$) and then also reported the marked angle, $4(19.6) + 12$, instead of the angle asked for.
Found the $92^\circ$ angle and subtracted it from 90 (getting $-2$, entered as 2), using a complement instead of the supplement along a straight line.

stem: What is the greatest possible value of this sum, in degrees?
stimulus: A sheet of laminated composite has two parallel fiber layers, which appear as straight parallel lines in a cross-section. A straight crack crosses both layers, forming eight angles at the two crossing points. One of these eight angles measures $64^\circ$. A technician picks four of the eight angles, including at least one acute angle, and adds their measures.
explanation: A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes only two distinct angle measures. One of them is $64^\circ$ and the other is $180 - 64 = 116^\circ$. Four of the eight angles are $64^\circ$ and four are $116^\circ$. If the four chosen angles include $a$ acute ones, the sum is $64a + 116(4 - a) = 464 - 52a$. The sum gets larger as $a$ gets smaller, and the condition requires $a \ge 1$. So the greatest sum uses one $64^\circ$ angle and three $116^\circ$ angles: $64 + 3(116) = 412$.

common_errors.why: Picked all four obtuse angles, $4(116)$, and ignored the requirement that at least one chosen angle be acute.
Picked all four acute angles, $4(64)$, which gives the least possible sum instead of the greatest.
Assumed the four angles must be two acute and two obtuse (or that any four angles 'fill a point'), and gave $2(64) + 2(116)$.
Mixed up the counts and used three acute angles and one obtuse angle: $3(64) + 116$.

Took the other angle measure as the complement, $90 - 64 = 26^\circ$, and computed $64 + 3(26) + \dots$ by using 26 in place of 116, getting $64 + 3(26) = 142$ or similar; the commonest form is $4(26) + 64 - 8 = 160$. The root error is using 90 instead of 180.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of each of the other two angles?
stimulus: At an observatory, two laser guide-star beams travel along straight lines that cross at point $P$, forming four angles. Two of these angles are vertical angles. One measures $(7x - 18)^\circ$ and the other measures $(3x + 42)^\circ$.
explanation: Vertical angles are equal, so $7x - 18 = 3x + 42$. Then $4x = 60$ and $x = 15$, so each of the two vertical angles measures $7(15) - 18 = 87^\circ$. Each of the other two angles forms a linear pair with an $87^\circ$ angle, so each measures $180 - 87 = 93^\circ$.

common_errors.why: Found the measure of the given vertical angles and reported that instead of the other two angles.
Stopped after solving for x.
Set the two expressions as supplementary: $10x + 24 = 180$ gives $x = 15.6$, a given angle of $91.2^\circ$, and a remaining angle of $180 - 91.2 = 88.8$.
Found the $87^\circ$ angle and subtracted it from 90 instead of 180.
Subtracted the $174^\circ$ total of the two given angles from 360, getting 186, and gave that combined total instead of dividing it between the two equal angles.

stimulus: In a bridge truss, an upper girder and a lower girder are straight and parallel. A straight diagonal brace connects them. Both angles in question are between the two girders and on the same side of the brace. The angle the brace makes with the upper girder measures $(2x + 25)^\circ$, and the angle it makes with the lower girder measures $(3x - 5)^\circ$.
explanation: Both angles lie between the parallel girders and on the same side of the brace, so they are same-side (co-interior) angles. Same-side interior angles are supplementary, not equal: $(2x + 25) + (3x - 5) = 180$. This gives $5x + 20 = 180$, so $5x = 160$ and $x = 32$. Check: the angles are $89^\circ$ and $91^\circ$, which add to $180^\circ$.

common_errors.why: Treated the same-side interior angles as equal: $2x + 25 = 3x - 5$ gives $x = 30$. Because both real angles are close to $90^\circ$, this looks believable.
Set the sum equal to 90 instead of 180: $5x + 20 = 90$ gives $x = 14$.
Solved correctly and then gave the angle at the upper girder, $2(32) + 25$, instead of x.
Solved correctly and then gave the angle at the lower girder, $3(32) - 5$, instead of x.
Mishandled the constants when combining them ($25 + 5 = 30$ instead of $25 - 5 = 20$): $5x - 30 + \dots$, giving $5x = 200$ and $x = 40$.
